claim: Hedgehog (Hh) and Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs) pattern the developing Drosophila wing by functioning as short- and long-range morphogens, respectively.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) and Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs) pattern the developing Drosophila wing by functioning as short- and long-range morphogens, respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Lecuit et al., 1996; Mullor et al., 1997; Nellen et al., 1996; Strigini and Cohen, 1997; Zecca et al., 1995) as indicated in the Introduction.

claim: nord is a novel target gene of the Hh signaling pathway identified through genome-wide expression profiling of Drosophila wing imaginal discs.
source: Through genome-wide expression profiling of the Drosophila wing imaginal discs, we identify nord as a novel target gene of the Hh signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data comparing gene expression in different cell populations (A, B, P cells) and confirmed by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nord is related to the vertebrate Neuron-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (NDNF) involved in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and several types of cancer.
source: Nord is related to the vertebrate Neuron-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (NDNF) involved in congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and several types of cancer.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior work (Boehm et al., 2015; Lima Amato et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019) in the Discussion.

claim: Loss of nord results in reduced wing growth and ectopic crossvein patterning in adult Drosophila wings.
source: Loss- and gain-of-function analyses implicate Nord in the regulation of wing growth and proper crossvein patterning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic analysis of nord mutant alleles (nordMI06414, nord22A, nord3D) showing reduced wing size and ectopic posterior crossvein formation as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nord is a secreted BMP-binding protein that localizes to the extracellular matrix.
source: At the molecular level, we present biochemical evidence that Nord is a secreted BMP-binding protein and localizes to the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot analysis showing Nord secretion in cell culture medium (Figure 3B), immunostaining showing extracellular localization (Figure 3C-E), and co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrating binding to Dpp and Gbb (Figure 8A).

claim: Nord binds to Decapentaplegic (Dpp) or the heterodimer Dpp-Glass-bottom boat (Gbb) to modulate their release and activity.
source: Nord binds to Decapentaplegic (Dpp) or the heterodimer Dpp-Glass-bottom boat (Gbb) to modulate their release and activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation assays showing Nord binding to Dpp and Gbb (Figure 8A), and by experiments showing that Nord co-expression reduces BMP ligand release into medium (Figure 8B).

claim: Nord is a dosage-dependent BMP modulator, where low levels of Nord promote and high levels inhibit BMP signaling.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that Nord is a dosage-dependent BMP modulator, where low levels of Nord promote and high levels inhibit BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments showing that loss of nord reduces pMad in larval discs but increases pMad in pupal wings (Figure 5), and by dose-dependent effects of ectopic Nord expression on PCV formation (Figure 7) and in vitro signaling assays (Figure 8F-I).

claim: Hh-induced Nord expression fine-tunes both the range and strength of BMP signaling in the developing Drosophila wing.
source: Taken together, we propose that Hh-induced Nord expression fine-tunes both the range and strength of BMP signaling in the developing Drosophila wing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations that nord is a Hh target gene (Figures 1-2), Nord modulates BMP signaling in a dose-dependent manner (Figures 5-8), and Nord affects both local and long-range BMP activity (Figure 9).

claim: In the wing discs, Hh is secreted in the posterior (P) compartment and spreads toward the anterior (A) compartment.
source: In the wing discs, Hh is secreted in the posterior (P) compartment and spreads toward the anterior (A) compartment (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Capdevila et al., 1994; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing the Hh expression pattern and signaling in wing discs.

claim: Hh signaling does not occur in P compartment cells because they do not express critical components of the Hh pathway, such as the major transcriptional effector Ci.
source: Hh signaling does not occur in P compartment cells because they do not express critical components of the Hh pathway, such as the major transcriptional effector Ci (Eaton and Kornberg, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by Ci immunostaining in Figure 1A showing Ci expression only in anterior compartment.

claim: A compartment cells can receive and respond to Hh but are unable to produce Hh.
source: Conversely, A compartment cells can receive and respond to Hh but are unable to produce Hh.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hh signaling in wing discs, supported by the expression patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hh activates the localized expression of several target genes, including ptc and decapentaplegic (dpp).
source: Hh synthesized by P cells diffuses into the A compartment adjacent to the A/P boundary, where it is sequestered by the Ptc-Ihog/Boi receptor complex (Chen and Struhl, 1996; Zheng et al., 2010), thus forming a short-range gradient that activates the localized expression ofseveral target genes, including ptc and decapentaplegic (dpp) (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Capdevila et al., 1994; Chen and Struhl, 1996; Ingham et al., 1991; Tabata and Kornberg, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work and confirmed by expression analysis in Figure 1.

claim: Dpp is the homolog of vertebrate TGF-β superfamily ligands BMP2/4.
source: Dpp is the homolog of vertebrate TGF-β superfamily ligands BMP2/4, which binds to the BMP type I receptor thickveins (Tkv) or Saxophone (Sax) and type II receptor Punt (Parker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Upon ligand binding, Tkv or Sax phosphorylates the transcription factor Mad (referred to as pMad; an indication of active Dpp signal transduction).
source: Upon ligand binding, Tkv or Sax phosphorylates the transcription factor Mad (referred to as pMad; an indication of active Dpp signal transduction).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMP signaling pathway, supported by citation (Moustakas and Heldin, 2009).

claim: Phosphorylated Mad forms a trimeric complex with the co-Smad Medea and is translocated to the nucleus where it regulates downstream target genes.
source: Phosphorylated Mad then forms a trimeric complex with the co-Smad Medea and is translocated to the nucleus where it regulates downstream target genes (Moustakas and Heldin, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMP signaling pathway, supported by citation.

claim: Dpp diffuses into both the A and P compartments and acts as a long-range morphogen.
source: In contrast to the Hh signal, Dpp diffuses into both the A and P compartments and acts as a long-range morphogen (Brook et al., 1996; Lawrence and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by pMad staining patterns shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Dpp has multiple roles both in determining the wing size by promoting growth and epithelial morphogenesis during larval stages.
source: Dpp has multiple roles both in determining the wing size by promoting growth and epithelial morphogenesis during larval stages (Gibson and Perrimon, 2005; Schwank et al., 2008; Shen and Dahmann, 2005), and in patterning the longitudinal veins (LV) as well as the anterior crossvein (ACV) and posterior crossvein (PCV) during pupal development (de Celis et al., 1996; Ralston and Blair, 2005; Serpe et al., 2005; Shimmi et al., 2005; Sotillos and De Celis, 2005; Vilmos et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The BMP family ligand Glass-bottom boat (Gbb) can form heterodimers with Dpp to augment the level and increase the range of BMP signaling in different cells and tissues.
source: In Drosophila, two other characterized BMP family ligands, the BMP5/6/7/8 homolog Glass-bottom boat (Gbb), and the more distantly related Screw (Scw) (Arora et al., 1994; Padgett et al., 1987; Wharton et al., 1991), can form heterodimers with Dpp to augment the level and increase the range of BMP signaling in different cells and tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8A showing Dpp-Gbb heterodimer formation.

claim: Short gastrulation (Sog), Twisted gastrulation (Tsg), Crossveinless (Cv), Crossveinless-2 (Cv-2), Larval translucida (ltl), Pentagone (Pent), Kekkon5 (Kek5), Dally and Dally-like protein (Dlp) have been identified as modulators that enhance or inhibit BMP signaling.
source: Other secreted or membrane-binding BMP-binding proteins, including Short gastrulation (Sog) (Ralston and Blair, 2005; Serpe et al., 2005), Twisted gastrulation (Tsg), Crossveinless (Cv) (Shimmi et al., 2005; Vilmos et al., 2005), Crossveinless-2 (Cv-2) (Conley et al., 2000; Serpe et al., 2008), Larval translucida (ltl) (Szuperák et al., 2011), Pentagone (Pent) (Vuilleumier et al., 2010), Kekkon5 (Kek5) (Evans et al., 2009), Dally and Dally-like protein (Dlp) (Akiyama et al., 2008; Belenkaya et al., 2004), have been identified as modulators that enhance or inhibit BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Tkv critically affects Dpp tissue distribution through ligand trapping and internalization, and thus globally shapes the BMP activity gradient.
source: Additionally, Tkv, the main type I Dpp receptor in Drosophila, critically affects Dpp tissue distribution through ligand trapping and internalization, and thus globally shapes the BMP activity gradient (Crickmore and Mann, 2006; Lecuit and Cohen, 1998; Tanimoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Hh signal simultaneously induces Dpp expression and lowers responsiveness to Dpp in the same cells at the A/P border by repressing transcription of the tkv receptor gene.
source: Prominent among the many determinants that impact proper establishment and maintenance of the Dpp activity gradient is the action of the Hh signal, which simultaneously induces Dpp expression and lowers responsiveness to Dpp in the same cells at the A/P border by repressing transcription of the tkv receptor gene (Tanimoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: nord transcripts were absent from the P compartment and primarily detected in the A cells adjacent to the A/P compartment boundary.
source: Like the known Hh signaling target gene ptc (Figure 1E and F), nord transcripts were absent from the P compartment and primarily detected in the A cells adjacent to the A/P compartment boundary (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1E) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1F).

claim: Unlike ptc and most other Hh pathway target genes, nord expression was not detected in the central wing pouch.
source: Of note, unlike ptc and most other Hh pathway target genes, nord expression was not detected in the central wing pouch (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 1F and immunostaining of Nord-GFP in Figure 2B.

claim: The Drosophila nord gene is associated with only one protein-coding transcript and one polypeptide containing 587 amino acids.
source: The Drosophila nord gene is associated with only one protein-coding transcript and one polypeptide containing 587 amino acids.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the nord gene structure and sequence as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A.

claim: Nord has a single homolog in the mouse genome, called NDNF.
source: It has a single homolog in the mouse genome, called NDNF (Kuang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nord and NDNF belong to a family of evolutionarily conserved secreted proteins with a predicted signal peptide followed by one or two fibronectin type III-like repeats (FN3) and a domain of unknown function (pfam10179: DUF2369).
source: Nord and NDNF belong to a family of evolutionarily conserved secreted proteins with a predicted signal peptide followed by one or two fibronectin type III-like repeats (FN3) and a domain of unknown function (pfam10179: DUF2369).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nearly all bilaterian animals have either single or multiple orthologous genes for Nord/Ndnf.
source: Analyses of the genome and EST sequences from various organisms suggest that nearly all bilaterian animals have either single or multiple orthologous genes for Nord/Ndnf (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both Nord and various NDNF proteins were secreted into the medium after transient transfection into HEK 293T cells.
source: We cloned the full-length cDNAs from Drosophila Nord and NDNF from several different species into a mammalian expression vector and found that both Nord and various NDNF proteins were secreted into the medium after transient transfection into HEK 293T cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of medium and cell lysate fractions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A significant amount of Nord/NDNF proteins was detected on the surface of transfected cells and the surrounding extracellular matrix within several cell diameters.
source: We immunostained unpermeabilized HEK 293T cells that were co-transfected with plasmids expressing Myc-tagged Nord or various NDNFs together with cytoplasmic-localized GFP proteins and detected a significant amount of Nord/NDNF proteins on the surface of the transfected cells (marked by cytoplasmic GFP expression), as well as the surrounding extracellular matrix within several cell diameters (Figure 3C, arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining of non-permeabilized cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Secreted Nord-GFP was noticed both flanking the A/P boundary and throughout the wing disc albeit at a much lower level when wing imaginal discs were immunostained in the absence of detergent.
source: Consistent with the observations in cultured cells, when wing imaginal discs from third instar larvae carrying nord-GFP were immunostained in the absence of detergent, secreted Nord-GFP was noticed both flanking the A/P boundary and throughout the wing disc albeit at a much lower level (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining without detergent shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Secreted Nord was detected outside of flip-out clones expressing HA-tagged Nord in wing imaginal discs.
source: Furthermore, when flip-out clones expressing an HA-tagged Nord were induced in the third instar wing imaginal discs, secreted Nord was detected outside of flip-out clones (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining without detergent shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Nord and its homolog NDNF belong to a family of secreted proteins, which likely exist in two spatially distinct pools: diffusible Nord/NDNF proteins that can reach a longer distance and membrane/matrix-associated Nord/NDNF proteins near the source cells.
source: Together, these data demonstrated that Nord and its homolog NDNF belong to a family of secreted proteins, which likely exist in two spatially distinct pools: diffusible Nord/NDNF proteins that can reach a longer distance and membrane/matrix-associated Nord/NDNF proteins near the source cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of secretion (Figure 3B), extracellular matrix association (Figure 3C-E), and diffusion beyond expressing cells (Figure 3C, E).

claim: Animals homozygous or trans-heterozygous for nord22A and nord3D are viable and fertile.
source: Animals homozygous or trans-heterozygous for nord22A and nord3D are viable and fertile.
evidence: This is an observation from genetic analysis of nord mutant alleles.

claim: A consistent and significant decrease in wing size was observed in both male and female flies homozygous or trans-heterozygous for nord22A and nord3D.
source: However, a consistent and significant decrease in wing size was observed in both male and female flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wing size measurements shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 61% of females and 21% of males of the nord22A allele showed ectopic venation in the vicinity of the PCV of one or both wings.
source: Along with the growth defects in the wing, we also noted that 61% of females (59/97) and 21% (17/82) of males of the nord22A allele showed ectopic venation in the vicinity of the PCV of one or both wings (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of ectopic venation phenotype shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 86% of nordMI06414 mutant females and 36% of mutant males showed additional vein material at one or both wings.
source: Like nord22A, the ectopic venation displayed higher penetrance in females than in males, with 86% of mutant females and 36% of mutant males showing additional vein material at one or both wings (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of ectopic venation phenotype shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ectopic venation phenotype was not observed in nord3D homozygotes.
source: This ectopic venation phenotype was not observed in nord3D homozygotes.
evidence: This is an observation from phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: All available deficiency lines in which the nord locus was entirely removed did not rescue the ectopic PCV phenotype of nordM106414.
source: All available deficiency lines in which the nord locus was entirely removed did not rescue the ectopic PCV phenotype of nordM106414, whereas adjacent deficiency lines with an intact nord locus fully rescued the crossvein defects in the nordMI06414 adult wings (Figure 4D and E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by complementation tests shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: nord22A in trans to Df(2R)BSC155 exhibited high-frequency ectopic venation (69% females and 26% males).
source: We next tested Df(2R)BSC155 in trans to either nord22A and nord3D and once again found that nord22A exhibited high-frequency ectopic venation (Figure 4D and E; 69% females and 26% males), while nord3D showed a modest interaction (14% females and <1% males).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of ectopic venation phenotype shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both nord22A and nord3D in trans to Df(2R)BSC155 produced smaller wings compared to controls.
source: Similar to the homozygotes, both nord22A and nord3D in trans to Df(2R)BSC155 also produced smaller wings compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wing size measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: No difference in wing trichome density was found for nord MI06414/Df(2R)BSC155 or nord22A/Df(2R)BSC155 compared to heterozygous controls.
source: To examine whether this size difference was the result of reduced cell proliferation or a smaller cell size, we examined wing trichome density as a proxy for cell size (Brummel et al., 1999; Dobzhansky, 1929; Martín-Castellanos and Edgar, 2002). We found no difference for nord MI06414/Df(2R)BSC155 or nord22A/Df(2R)BSC155 compared to heterozygous (nord MI06414/+ or nord22A/+) controls (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6), suggesting that the alteration in wing size is caused by reduced cell proliferation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by trichome density measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: The alteration in wing size in nord mutants is caused by reduced cell proliferation.
source: We found no difference for nord MI06414/Df(2R)BSC155 or nord22A/Df(2R)BSC155 compared to heterozygous (nord MI06414/+ or nord22A/+) controls (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6), suggesting that the alteration in wing size is caused by reduced cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that trichome density (a proxy for cell size) is unchanged, suggesting cell number rather than cell size is affected.

claim: Nord is required in wing imaginal discs for both proper growth and crossvein patterning.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that Nord is required in wing imaginal discs for both proper growth and crossvein patterning and that the nord3D allele may retain some function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined phenotypic analysis of multiple nord alleles showing wing size reduction and ectopic crossvein formation (Figure 4).

claim: The nord3D allele may retain some function.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that Nord is required in wing imaginal discs for both proper growth and crossvein patterning and that the nord3D allele may retain some function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nord3D does not show ectopic crossvein phenotype unlike other nord alleles (Figure 4E).

claim: Both Nord protein and Dpp precursor protein were present along the A/P boundary flanking the central wing pouch through the larval stage.
source: Both Nord protein indicated by the Nord-GFP fusion derived from the nord-GFP protein-trap allele and Dpp precursor protein detected via an anti-Dpp prodomain antibody were present along the A/P boundary flanking the central wing pouch through the larval stage (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunostaining of Nord-GFP and Dpp prodomain shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the pupal wing, both Nord and Dpp expression does not change during the first 8 hr after pupation (AP).
source: In the pupal wing, both Nord and Dpp expression does not change during the first 8 hr after pupation (AP) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining at different time points shown in Figure 5A.

claim: dpp disappears from the A/P boundary and commences expression in the differentiating LVs after 8 hr AP.
source: Subsequently, dpp disappears from the A/P boundary and commences expression in the differentiating LVs (deCelis, 1997; Yu et al., 1996); however, the Hh-dependent expression of nord along the A/P boundary remains for about 30 hr after pupation and diminishes after Dpp expression was detectable in both the LV and PCV regions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining at different time points shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Hh-dependent expression of nord along the A/P boundary remains for about 30 hr after pupation and diminishes after Dpp expression was detectable in both the LV and PCV regions.
source: Subsequently, dpp disappears from the A/P boundary and commences expression in the differentiating LVs (deCelis, 1997; Yu et al., 1996); however, the Hh-dependent expression of nord along the A/P boundary remains for about 30 hr after pupation and diminishes after Dpp expression was detectable in both the LV and PCV regions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining at different time points shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nord proteins secreted from the A/P boundary stripe are expressed together or in close proximity with Dpp through the larval and early pupal (0–30 hr AP) stages.
source: Taken together, Nord proteins secreted from the A/P boundary stripe are expressed together or in close proximity with Dpp through the larval and early pupal (0–30 hr AP) stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization studies shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pMad intensity was slightly reduced in nord mutant wing discs, and this reduction of pMad levels was more evident in the A compartment where Nord is expressed.
source: We quantified pMad signal intensity in nord mutant wing discs and compared it to that of wild-type controls. We found that the pMad intensity was slightly reduced in nord mutant wing discs, and this reduction of pMad levels was more evident in the A compartment where Nord is expressed (Figure 5B and C, arrow).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: No obvious difference in the Hh signaling activity was found in the wild-type and nord mutant discs.
source: In contrast, by measuring the expression of high-threshold target gene ptc and low-threshold gene dpp, we found no obvious difference in the Hh signaling activity in the wild-type and nord mutant discs (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ptc and Dpp immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 5B, C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No specific reduction in the L3–L4 region was found in nord mutant wings based on comparable or higher dL3–L4/dL2–L5 ratio.
source: When quantifying the distance between distal ends of LVs L3 and L4 (dL3–L4) and that of L2 and L5 (dL2–L5), we found no specific reduction in the L3–L4 region indicated by comparable or higher dL3–L4/dL2–L5 ratio in the female and male nord mutant wings (Figure 4B and C), which is consistent with normal Hh signaling activity during the development of nord mutant wing imaginal discs (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wing vein distance measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Endogenous Nord plays a positive role in augmenting BMP signaling activity to promote wing growth.
source: Together, these findings suggested a positive role of endogenous Nord in augmenting BMP signaling activity to promote wing growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of nord reduces pMad levels in larval wing discs (Figure 5B, C) and results in smaller wings (Figure 4C).

claim: A broadened pMad domain around the presumptive PCV was detected in nord mutants from 19 to 20 hr AP.
source: In contrast to the rather restricted pMad domain in wild-type pupal wings, we detected a broadened pMad domain around the presumptive PCV in nord mutants from 19 to 20 hr AP (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and quantification in pupal wings shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The ectopic pMad accumulation in nord mutants became an expanded patch adjacent to the presumptive PCV, indicating that BMP signaling was abnormally elevated in this region.
source: Gradually, the ectopic pMad accumulation became an expanded patch adjacent to the presumptive PCV, indicating that BMP signaling was abnormally elevated in this region (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining at later time points shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Nord expression was not seen in the LV or primordia PCV during early pupal stage.
source: During early pupal stage, it is notable that Nord expression was seen neither in the LV nor primordia PCV (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Nord-GFP immunostaining in pupal wings shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No ectopic PCV was noticed in adult flies when UAS-nord-RNAi was selectively expressed in the P compartment of the larval and pupal wing via the hh-Gal4 driver.
source: In agreement, we did not notice any ectopic PCV in the adult flies when UAS-nord-RNAi was selectively expressed in the P compartment of the larval and pupal wing via the hh-Gal4 driver (Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Nord proteins secreted from the A/P boundary would likely play a role in reducing excessive BMP signaling in the L4–L5 intervein region to prevent ectopic venation.
source: Given that Nord is a secreted protein (Figure 3), Nord proteins secreted from the A/P boundary would likely play a role in reducing excessive BMP signaling in the L4–L5 intervein region to prevent ectopic venation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nord mutants show ectopic PCV (Figure 4D, E) and increased pMad in the PCV region (Figure 5D, E), combined with the fact that Nord is secreted (Figure 3).

claim: Ectopic venation phenotype was observed when nord was selectively knocked down in the Hh-responding cells using ptc-Gal4.
source: To test this possibility, we analyzed the ectopic venation phenotype in flies carrying ptc-Gal4-driven expression of UAS-nord-RNAi. Although ectopic venation phenotype was observed when nord was selectively knocked down in the Hh-responding cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), the frequency of flies carrying ectopic PCV was lower when compared to nord mutant flies (Figure 4D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The frequency of flies carrying ectopic PCV was lower in ptc-Gal4>UAS-nord-RNAi compared to nord mutant flies.
source: Although ectopic venation phenotype was observed when nord was selectively knocked down in the Hh-responding cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), the frequency of flies carrying ectopic PCV was lower when compared to nord mutant flies (Figure 4D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The weaker phenotype in ptc-Gal4>UAS-nord-RNAi likely resulted from residual Nord protein either due to incomplete knock down or due to possible Nord expression and secretion from other tissues.
source: This weaker phenotype likely resulted from residual Nord protein either due to incomplete ptc-Gal4>UAS-nord-RNAi-mediated nord knock down in the cells flanking the A/P boundary or due to possible Nord expression and secretion from other tissues.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of weaker phenotype in RNAi knockdown compared to genetic mutants.

claim: Endogenous Nord plays a negative role in inhibiting BMP signaling activity in the early pupal wing to prevent the formation of ectopic crossveins in the posterior compartment.
source: Nevertheless, opposite to the positive role of enhancing BMP signaling activity to promote growth of the larval wing discs, endogenous Nord also plays a negative role in inhibiting BMP signaling activity in the early pupal wing to prevent the formation of ectopic crossveins in the posterior compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nord mutants show ectopic PCV (Figure 4D, E) and increased pMad in the PCV region (Figure 5D, E).

claim: Ectopic Nord expression resulted in reduced range and level of the pMad gradient in the third instar wing imaginal discs.
source: Under control of the ubiquitous wing blade driver nub-Gal4, ectopic Nord expression resulted in reduced range and level of the pMad gradient in the third instar wing imaginal discs (Figure 6A and B, 25°C), and accordingly decreased wing size in both adult males and females (Figure 6C and D, 25°C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and quantification (Figure 6A, B) and wing size measurements (Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Ectopic Nord expression decreased wing size in both adult males and females.
source: Under control of the ubiquitous wing blade driver nub-Gal4, ectopic Nord expression resulted in reduced range and level of the pMad gradient in the third instar wing imaginal discs (Figure 6A and B, 25°C), and accordingly decreased wing size in both adult males and females (Figure 6C and D, 25°C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by wing size measurements shown in Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In animals raised at 29°C expressing higher levels of exogenous Nord, both a much reduced pMad gradient in the larval wing discs and more severely decreased wing size in the adult flies were detected.
source: Indeed, in animals raised at 29°C expressing higher levels of exogenous Nord, we detected both a much reduced pMad gradient in the larval wing discs and more severely decreased wing size in the adult flies (Figure 6A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and quantification (Figure 6A, B) and wing size measurements (Figure 6C, D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) at different temperatures.

claim: Hh signaling activity is relatively normal in the wing discs expressing ectopic Nord.
source: In contrast, Hh signaling activity is relatively normal in the wing discs expressing ectopic Nord. Although the Ptc-expressing domain became narrower, we did not notice any obvious decrease in the levels of Ptc expression. (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ptc immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Ectopic Nord expression did not cause any specific reduction in the distance of L3 and L4 based on the dL3–L4/dL2–L5 ratio.
source: Consistently, ectopic Nord expression did not cause any specific reduction in the distance of L3 and L4 based on the dL3–L4/dL2–L5 ratio (Figure 6D), suggesting that the wing growth defect caused by ectopic Nord is unlikely due to inhibition of Hh signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by wing vein distance measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The wing growth defect caused by ectopic Nord is unlikely due to inhibition of Hh signaling.
source: Consistently, ectopic Nord expression did not cause any specific reduction in the distance of L3 and L4 based on the dL3–L4/dL2–L5 ratio (Figure 6D), suggesting that the wing growth defect caused by ectopic Nord is unlikely due to inhibition of Hh signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the L3-L4 region is not specifically affected (Figure 6D) and Ptc expression is normal (Figure 6A, B).

claim: Partial L5 and PCV loss was noticed in the wings with more dramatic size reduction caused by ectopic Nord expression.
source: Interestingly, partial L5 and PCV loss was also noticed in the wings with more dramatic size reduction (Figure 6C, arrowheads and arrows), and the frequency of disrupted L5 and PCV was more dramatic when the flies were raised at higher temperatures and expressed higher levels of ectopic Nord (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The frequency of disrupted L5 and PCV was more dramatic when the flies were raised at higher temperatures and expressed higher levels of ectopic Nord.
source: Interestingly, partial L5 and PCV loss was also noticed in the wings with more dramatic size reduction (Figure 6C, arrowheads and arrows), and the frequency of disrupted L5 and PCV was more dramatic when the flies were raised at higher temperatures and expressed higher levels of ectopic Nord (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of adult wing phenotypes at different temperatures shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ectopic Nord attenuates BMP signaling, leading to inhibition of wing growth and vein patterning.
source: Therefore, our observations indicate that ectopic Nord attenuates BMP signaling, leading to inhibition of wing growth and vein patterning.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations that ectopic Nord reduces pMad (Figure 6A, B), decreases wing size (Figure 6C, D), and causes vein loss (Figure 6C).

claim: Nord has both positive and negative effects in modulating BMP signaling activity, where low (endogenous) levels of Nord enhance and high (ectopic) levels of Nord inhibit BMP signaling.
source: Along with the positive role of endogenous Nord in enhancing BMP signaling to promote wing growth, we propose a model that Nord has both positive and negative effects in modulating BMP signaling activity, where low (endogenous) levels of Nord enhance and high (ectopic) levels of Nord inhibit BMP signaling.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined observations from loss-of-function (Figures 4-5) and gain-of-function (Figures 6-7) experiments.

claim: Activation of UAS-Nord expression by temperature shifts at 78 hr or earlier before eclosion caused the most severe PCV phenotype.
source: We found that activation of UAS-Nord expression by temperature shifts at 78 hr or earlier before eclosion caused the most severe PCV phenotype, but activation at 66 hr before eclosion or later resulted in essentially normal PCV (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal expression experiments and phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 7B, C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of UAS-Nord expression at 66 hr before eclosion or later resulted in essentially normal PCV.
source: We found that activation of UAS-Nord expression by temperature shifts at 78 hr or earlier before eclosion caused the most severe PCV phenotype, but activation at 66 hr before eclosion or later resulted in essentially normal PCV (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal expression experiments and phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 7B, C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The abnormal PCV phenotypes relied on the levels of exogenous Nord: expression of a lower level of Nord (1XUAS-Nord) led to ectopic PCV, moderate levels (2XUAS-Nord) yielded a mixed phenotype with both ectopic and slightly reduced PCV, whereas high levels (3XUAS-Nord) gave rise to nearly complete loss of PCV.
source: More importantly, we found that the abnormal PCV phenotypes relied on the levels of exogenous Nord: expression of a lower level of Nord (1XUAS-Nord) led to ectopic PCV, moderate levels (2XUAS-Nord) yielded a mixed phenotype with both ectopic and slightly reduced PCV, whereas high levels (3XUAS-Nord) gave rise to nearly complete loss of PCV (Figure 7B and C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-dependent phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 7B, C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exogenous Nord expressed within the hh-Gal4 or en-Gal4-expressing domains was able to influence crossvein patterning in the A compartment although with a lower frequency.
source: Of note, consistent with the fact that Nord is a secreted protein, exogenous Nord expressed within the hh-Gal4 or en-Gal4-expressing domains was also able to influence crossvein patterning in the A compartment although with a lower frequency (Figure 7B, blue arrows and blue arrowheads, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The critical time window in which the primordial PCV responds to exogenously expressed Nord (66–78 hr before eclosion at 29°C) coincides with the stage during which BMP signaling induces PCV formation.
source: The critical time window in which the primordial PCV responds to exogenously expressed Nord (66–78 hr before eclosion at 29°C) coincides with the stage during which BMP signaling induces PCV formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression experiments (Figure 7A-C) and known timing of PCV formation.

claim: Adult PCV defects and pMad patterns in pupal wings showed a correlation with the level of ectopic Nord.
source: As shown in Figure 7D, adult PCV defects and pMad patterns in pupal wings showed a correlation with the level of ectopic Nord, where the temperature shift occurred 12 hr after the start of pupal development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation between Nord expression levels and pMad/PCV phenotypes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In pupal wings expressing a low level of exogenous Nord (1XUAS-Nord), ectopic pMad and ectopic crossveins were detected.
source: In pupal wings expressing a low level of exogenous Nord (1XUAS-Nord), ectopic pMad and ectopic crossveins were detected, while moderate overexpression (2XUAS-Nord) led to a mixed phenotype of partial pMad and crossvein vein loss or wider pMad and ectopic veins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Moderate overexpression of Nord (2XUAS-Nord) led to a mixed phenotype of partial pMad and crossvein vein loss or wider pMad and ectopic veins.
source: In pupal wings expressing a low level of exogenous Nord (1XUAS-Nord), ectopic pMad and ectopic crossveins were detected, while moderate overexpression (2XUAS-Nord) led to a mixed phenotype of partial pMad and crossvein vein loss or wider pMad and ectopic veins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: When high Nord levels (3XUAS-Nord) were expressed in the pupal wings, pMad and the PCV were largely absent.
source: When high Nord levels (3XUAS-Nord) were expressed in the pupal wings, pMad and the PCV were largely absent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad immunostaining and adult wing phenotypes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The level of Nord influences the outcome of PCV patterning during the early pupal development where a lower level of exogenous Nord resulted in enhanced BMP signaling and ectopic PCV, while higher levels of exogenous Nord inhibited BMP signaling and caused disrupted or depleted PCVs.
source: Although the temporal resolution is somewhat limited, the results clearly indicate that the level of Nord influences the outcome of PCV patterning during the early pupal development where a lower level of exogenous Nord resulted in enhanced BMP signaling and ectopic PCV, while higher levels of exogenous Nord inhibited BMP signaling and caused disrupted or depleted PCVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent effects shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Nord co-precipitated with Dpp and, to a lesser extent, with Gbb.
source: We found that Nord co-precipitated with Dpp and, to a lesser extent, with Gbb (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: An increased level of Nord proteins co-precipitated with Dpp or Gbb when Dpp and Gbb were co-expressed.
source: Additionally, we observed an increased level of Nord proteins co-precipitated with Dpp or Gbb when Dpp and Gbb were co-expressed (Figure 8A), indicating that Nord may have a higher affinity for Dpp-Gbb heterodimers formed in cells co-expressing Dpp and Gbb.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Nord may have a higher affinity for Dpp-Gbb heterodimers formed in cells co-expressing Dpp and Gbb.
source: Additionally, we observed an increased level of Nord proteins co-precipitated with Dpp or Gbb when Dpp and Gbb were co-expressed (Figure 8A), indicating that Nord may have a higher affinity for Dpp-Gbb heterodimers formed in cells co-expressing Dpp and Gbb.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that more Nord co-precipitates when both Dpp and Gbb are present (Figure 8A).

claim: Far less cleaved Dpp protein was released into the conditioned medium when Nord was co-expressed.
source: We next collected conditioned medium from S2 cells expressing Dpp or Dpp-Gbb with or without co-expressed Nord (source cell) and compared the levels of processed Dpp or Dpp-Gbb within the different conditioned media. We found that far less cleaved Dpp protein was released into the conditioned medium when Nord was co-expressed (Figure 8B, compare lane M3 with M2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of conditioned medium shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The same negative effect of Nord on BMP ligand release was observed when the medium was collected from cells expressing both Dpp and Gbb.
source: Likewise, the same negative effect of Nord was observed when the medium was collected from cells expressing both Dpp and Gbb (Figure 8B, compare lane M5 with M4), albeit the increased total amount of ligands likely reflects the release of Dpp-Gbb heterodimers (Figure 8B, compare lane M4 with M2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of conditioned medium shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The presence of Nord affected the release into the media of both Dpp and Dpp-Gbb, likely via binding to the BMP ligand.
source: Thus, the presence of Nord affected the release into the media of both Dpp and Dpp-Gbb, likely via binding to the BMP ligand.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations that Nord binds BMPs (Figure 8A) and reduces their release (Figure 8B).

claim: Conditioned medium containing either Dpp or Dpp-Gbb, but not that containing Nord alone, was able to induce Mad phosphorylation.
source: Upon incubation of the Mad-S2 responding cells with conditioned medium collected from the source cells, BMP signaling activity was monitored by measuring the pMad signal intensity. Conditioned medium containing either Dpp or Dpp-Gbb, but not that containing Nord alone, was able to induce Mad phosphorylation (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of pMad in responding cells shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The conditioned medium collected from source cells co-expressing Nord showed lower pMad signal intensity compared to that collected from source cells lacking Nord co-expression.
source: In agreement with the dramatically reduced amount of Dpp or Dpp-Gbb ligands (Figure 8B), the conditioned medium collected from source cells co-expressing Nord showed lower pMad signal intensity compared to that collected from source cells lacking Nord co-expression (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of pMad in responding cells shown in Figure 8C and quantification in Figure 8D.

claim: The matrix-associated Nord may sequester Dpp and Dpp-Gbb ligands to the source cells and thereby reduce ligand level in the media, which in turn leads to decreased BMP signaling activity in the responding cells.
source: Of note, Nord is not a membrane-tethered protein (Figure 3A), but we observed noticeable amounts of Nord deposited on the surface of source cells, as well as the surrounding extracellular matrix (Figure 3C and D). Thus, the matrix-associated Nord may sequester Dpp and Dpp-Gbb ligands to the source cells and thereby reduce ligand level in the media, which in turn leads to decreased BMP signaling activity in the responding cells (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations that Nord associates with extracellular matrix (Figure 3C, D), binds BMPs (Figure 8A), reduces BMP release (Figure 8B), and decreases signaling activity (Figure 8C, D).

claim: When the signaling activity was normalized to the ligand amount, the relative ligand activity from the medium without Nord is lower than that with Nord.
source: However, when the signaling activity was further normalized to the ligand amount (Figure 8B), the relative ligand activity ([pMad/Mad]/BMPs) from the medium without Nord is lower than that with Nord (Figure 8E), suggesting that while ectopic Nord expressed in the source cells reduced the levels of released ligand, that soluble ligand appears to have a higher signaling activity perhaps as a result of an association with Nord (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of relative ligand activity shown in Figure 8E.

claim: While ectopic Nord expressed in the source cells reduced the levels of released ligand, that soluble ligand appears to have a higher signaling activity perhaps as a result of an association with Nord.
source: However, when the signaling activity was further normalized to the ligand amount (Figure 8B), the relative ligand activity ([pMad/Mad]/BMPs) from the medium without Nord is lower than that with Nord (Figure 8E), suggesting that while ectopic Nord expressed in the source cells reduced the levels of released ligand, that soluble ligand appears to have a higher signaling activity perhaps as a result of an association with Nord (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ligand-normalized signaling activity is higher in the presence of Nord (Figure 8E).

claim: In vitro, the lowest tested level of Nord enhanced signaling while higher Nord levels reduced Dpp signaling activity.
source: Consistent with our in vivo analyses, in vitro, we also observed a dosage-dependent signaling profile of rDpp in the presence of increasing concentrations of Nord where the lowest tested level of Nord enhanced signaling while higher Nord levels reduced Dpp signaling activity (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 8F and quantification in Figure 8G.

claim: The highest level of Nord supplied from conditional medium failed to completely inhibit the free rDpp-induced BMP signaling.
source: Notably, the highest level of Nord supplied from conditional medium failed to completely inhibit the free rDpp-induced BMP signaling.
evidence: This is an observation from the dose-response experiments shown in Figure 8F, G.

claim: Transient expression of Nord-GFP in the Mad-S2 cells partially inhibited the average Mad phosphorylation induced by exogenous rDpp.
source: We next transiently transfected Mad-S2 cells for expression of Nord-GFP. Similar to Nord supplied from conditioned medium, we found that transient expression of Nord-GFP in the Mad-S2 cells partially inhibited the average Mad phosphorylation induced by exogenous rDpp (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response experiments with transiently expressed Nord shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Cells expressing Nord-GFP exhibited much lower pMad when compared to the surrounding Mad-S2 cells lacking Nord-GFP expression.
source: Remarkably, immunofluorescent staining revealed that cells expressing Nord-GFP exhibited much lower pMad when compared to the surrounding Mad-S2 cells lacking Nord-GFP expression (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Cells expressing GFP did not cause a noticeable reduction in pMad level in rDpp-treated Mad-S2 cells.
source: In contrast, cells expressing GFP did not cause a noticeable reduction in pMad level in rDpp-treated Mad-S2 cells (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 8I.

claim: The much stronger cell-autonomous inhibition of Nord on BMP signaling is likely due to a much higher level of ectopic Nord when overexpressed in the Mad-S2 cells.
source: The much stronger cell-autonomous inhibition of Nord on BMP signaling is likely due to a much higher level of ectopic Nord when overexpressed in the Mad-S2 cells (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of stronger inhibition in transfected cells (Figure 8I) compared to conditioned medium treatment (Figure 8F-H).

claim: Both in vivo and in vitro assays demonstrated that Nord not only can sequester BMP ligands, thereby impeding their release from the source cells, but may also directly modulate the activity of released BMP ligands in a dosage-dependent manner, where low levels promote and high doses attenuate BMP signaling.
source: Taken together, both our in vivo and in vitro assays demonstrated that Nord not only can sequester BMP ligands, thereby impeding their release from the source cells, but may also directly modulate the activity of released BMP ligands in a dosage-dependent manner, where low levels promote and high doses attenuate BMP signaling.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined results from in vivo (Figures 4-7) and in vitro (Figure 8) experiments.

claim: The Hh signal shapes the activity gradient of BMP by both inducing the expression of Dpp and simultaneously downregulating the Dpp receptor Tkv, resulting in lower responsiveness to Dpp in cells at the A/P compartment border.
source: It has been previously shown that the Hh signal shapes the activity gradient of BMP by both inducing the expression of Dpp and simultaneously downregulating the Dpp receptor Tkv, resulting in lower responsiveness to Dpp in cells at the A/P compartment border (Tanimoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The activity of BMP is further fine-tuned by another previously unknown Hh-dependent mechanism involving induction of nord.
source: In this study, we showed that the activity of BMP is further fine-tuned by another previously unknown Hh-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined results showing nord is a Hh target gene (Figures 1-2) that modulates BMP signaling (Figures 4-8).

claim: Elimination of nord caused a reduction of overall wing size and resulted in ectopic PCV formation.
source: Elimination of nord caused a reduction of overall wing size and resulted in ectopic PCV formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic analysis of nord mutants shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both wing size reduction and ectopic PCV formation in nord mutants are attributable to alterations of BMP signaling activity as monitored by the level of Mad phosphorylation, yet in opposite directions.
source: Both of these phenotypes are attributable to alterations of BMP signaling activity as monitored by the level of Mad phosphorylation, yet in opposite directions: loss of nord led to decreased pMad in larval wing discs, whereas ectopic pMad surrounded the primordial PCV in nord mutant pupal wings (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pMad analysis in larval and pupal wings shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Expressing exogenous Nord at different levels and during different developmental stages and contexts showed that Nord is a dosage-dependent modulator of BMP signaling both in wing growth and crossvein patterning.
source: Moreover, expressing exogenous Nord at different levels and during different developmental stages and contexts showed that Nord is a dosage-dependent modulator of BMP signaling both in wing growth and crossvein patterning (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by gain-of-function experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Nord is a BMP-binding protein that directly enhances or inhibits BMP signaling in cultured S2 cells.
source: At the molecular level, we further demonstrated that Nord is a BMP-binding protein that directly enhances or inhibits BMP signaling in cultured S2 cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Nord mediates BMP signaling activity through binding of the BMP ligands Dpp and Dpp-Gbb.
source: Combining the genetic and biochemical evidence, we propose that Nord mediates BMP signaling activity through binding of the BMP ligands Dpp and Dpp-Gbb (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined genetic and biochemical evidence from Figures 4-8.

claim: Depending on the levels of Nord proteins and the source/types of BMP ligands, Nord-mediated binding of Dpp and Dpp-Gbb may promote or repress BMP signaling activity.
source: Depending on the levels of Nord proteins and the source/types of BMP ligands, Nord-mediated binding of Dpp and Dpp-Gbb may promote or repress BMP signaling activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the dose-dependent effects observed in Figures 5-8.

claim: The existence of two spatially distinct pools of diffusible and membrane/matrix-associated Nord proteins may introduce further complications in Nord-mediated BMP signaling regulation.
source: Additionally, the existence of two spatially distinct pools of diffusible and membrane/matrix-associated Nord proteins may introduce further complications in Nord-mediated BMP signaling regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of two pools of Nord (Figure 3) and their potential differential effects on BMP signaling.

claim: In the wild-type wing discs, expressed in a subset of Dpp-secreting cells along the A/P boundary, Nord binds and enhances the local BMP signaling activity by augmenting ligand concentration near the Nord/Dpp-secreting cells.
source: In the wild-type wing discs, expressed in a subset of Dpp-secreting cells along the A/P boundary, Nord binds and enhances the local BMP signaling activity by augmenting ligand concentration near the Nord/Dpp-secreting cells.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observation that loss of nord reduces pMad in the A compartment (Figure 5B, C) and Nord binds BMPs (Figure 8A).

claim: Nord impedes the mobilization of Dpp, especially the long-range BMP signaling mediator Dpp-Gbb heterodimer.
source: Meanwhile, Nord also impedes the mobilization of Dpp, especially the long-range BMP signaling mediator Dpp-Gbb heterodimer (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observation that Nord reduces BMP ligand release (Figure 8B) and has higher affinity for Dpp-Gbb heterodimers (Figure 8A).

claim: Loss of nord simultaneously led to reduced local BMP and increased long-range BMP activities, and therefore gave rise to the seemingly opposite phenotypes of reduced wing size and ectopic PCV.
source: Loss of nord simultaneously led to reduced local BMP and increased long-range BMP activities, and therefore gave rise to the seemingly opposite phenotypes of reduced wing size and ectopic PCV (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the dual phenotypes observed in nord mutants (Figures 4-5).

claim: Low levels of ectopic Nord in the P compartment autonomously increased BMP signaling activity.
source: In contrast, low levels of ectopic Nord in the P compartment autonomously increased BMP signaling activity (Figure 9C), whereas high levels of Nord, either in the P compartment or throughout the wing pouch, inhibited BMP signaling activity likely through interfering with the normal BMP reception (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-dependent effects of ectopic Nord shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: High levels of Nord, either in the P compartment or throughout the wing pouch, inhibited BMP signaling activity likely through interfering with the normal BMP reception.
source: In contrast, low levels of ectopic Nord in the P compartment autonomously increased BMP signaling activity (Figure 9C), whereas high levels of Nord, either in the P compartment or throughout the wing pouch, inhibited BMP signaling activity likely through interfering with the normal BMP reception (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-dependent effects of ectopic Nord shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: Hh-induced Nord expression provides an exquisite regulation of the strength and range of BMP signaling in the developing Drosophila wing.
source: Taken together, we propose that Hh-induced Nord expression provides an exquisite regulation of the strength and range of BMP signaling in the developing Drosophila wing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined observations that nord is a Hh target gene (Figures 1-2) that modulates BMP signaling in a dose-dependent manner (Figures 4-8).

claim: The Drosophila protein Nord is missing the first FN3 domain compared to vertebrate NDNFs.
source: Notably, the Drosophila protein is missing the first FN3 domain, and therefore it is not clear the extent to which Nord and the vertebrate NDNFs may exhibit functional conservation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: It is not clear the extent to which Nord and the vertebrate NDNFs may exhibit functional conservation.
source: Notably, the Drosophila protein is missing the first FN3 domain, and therefore it is not clear the extent to which Nord and the vertebrate NDNFs may exhibit functional conservation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural differences between Nord and vertebrate NDNFs (Figure 3A).

claim: The original human NDNF clone was identified on the basis of domain structure conservation with Drosophila Nord, which was identified via enhancer trapping to be a gene expressed in mushroom bodies and whose loss leads to defects in olfactory learning and memory.
source: Ironically, the original human NDNF clone was identified on the basis of domain structure conservation with Drosophila Nord, which was identified via enhancer trapping to be a gene expressed in mushroom bodies and whose loss leads to defects in olfactory learning and memory (Dubnau et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the mouse, NDNF is highly expressed in many neurons of the brain and spinal cord.
source: In the mouse, NDNF is highly expressed in many neurons of the brain and spinal cord (Boyle et al., 2011; Kuang et al., 2010; Schuman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Studies using cultured mouse hippocampal neurons revealed that NDNF promotes neuron migration and neurite outgrowth.
source: Studies using cultured mouse hippocampal neurons revealed that it promotes neuron migration and neurite outgrowth, hence its name (Kuang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NDNF was found to be upregulated in mouse endothelial cells in response to hindlimb ischemia, where it promotes endothelial cell and cardiomyocyte survival through integrin-mediated activation of AKT/endothelial NOS signaling.
source: In later studies, NDNF was also found to be upregulated in mouse endothelial cells in response to hindlimb ischemia, where it promotes endothelial cell and cardiomyocyte survival through integrin-mediated activation of AKT/endothelial NOS signaling (Ohashi et al., 2014; Joki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent studies have shown that NDNF expression is significantly downregulated in human lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC), indicating that NDNF may also provide a beneficial function as a tumor suppressor.
source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that NDNF expression is significantly downregulated in human lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC), indicating that NDNF may also provide a beneficial function as a tumor suppressor (Xia et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NDNF mutants were discovered in the genomes of several probands with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH), a rare genetic disorder that is characterized by absence of puberty, infertility, and anosmia (loss of smell).
source: Remarkably, NDNF mutants were discovered in the genomes of several probands with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH), a rare genetic disorder that is characterized by absence of puberty, infertility, and anosmia (loss of smell) (Boehm et al., 2015; Lima Amato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The CHH phenotype caused by NDNF mutations is very similar to that produced by loss of the anos1, which also encodes an FN3 superfamily member and is responsible for Kallmann syndrome.
source: This phenotype is very similar to that produced by loss of the anos1, which also encodes an FN3 superfamily member and is responsible for Kallmann syndrome, a condition that similarly presents with CHH and anosmia due to lack of proper GnRH and olfactory neuron migration (Stamou and Georgopoulos, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In vitro studies indicated that NDNF modulates FGFR1 signaling after FGF8 stimulation.
source: Although in vitro studies indicated that NDNF modulates FGFR1 signaling after FGF8 stimulation, the in vivo molecular mechanism responsible for the neuronal migration defects is not clear (Messina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The in vivo molecular mechanism responsible for the neuronal migration defects in NDNF mutants is not clear.
source: Although in vitro studies indicated that NDNF modulates FGFR1 signaling after FGF8 stimulation, the in vivo molecular mechanism responsible for the neuronal migration defects is not clear (Messina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The results of this study on the function of Drosophila Nord raise the issue of whether any of the ascribed vertebrate NDNF functions could involve alterations in BMP signaling.
source: The results of our study on the function of Drosophila Nord raise the issue of whether any of the ascribed vertebrate NDNF functions could involve alterations in BMP signaling.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings that Nord modulates BMP signaling in Drosophila (Figures 4-8).

claim: BMPs, as well as other TGF-β family members, participate at many levels in angiogenesis and EMT.
source: In the case of angiogenesis and EMT, BMPs, as well as other TGF-β family members, participate at many levels (Goumans et al., 2018; Kahata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At present, no involvement of BMP or TGF-β signaling has been implicated in migration of the GnRH neurons.
source: At present, however, no involvement of BMP or TGF-β signaling has been implicated in migration of the GnRH neurons, although BMP signaling does define neurogenic permissive areas in which the olfactory placode forms (Forni and Wray, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BMP signaling defines neurogenic permissive areas in which the olfactory placode forms.
source: At present, however, no involvement of BMP or TGF-β signaling has been implicated in migration of the GnRH neurons, although BMP signaling does define neurogenic permissive areas in which the olfactory placode forms (Forni and Wray, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A clear objective for the future is to determine if the vertebrate NDNF factors bind BMPs and/or HSPG proteins such as Dally-like glypicans to modulate BMP signaling activity.
source: A clear objective for the future is to determine if the vertebrate NDNF factors bind BMPs and/or HSPG proteins such as Dally-like glypicans to modulate BMP signaling activity.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions based on the findings in Drosophila.

claim: Additional non-BMP-modulating roles for Nord should also be examined in Drosophila.
source: On the Drosophila side, additional non-BMP-modulating roles for Nord should also be examined.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.
